# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.
You are an independent reviewer in Flint's ingest review gate. Another model wrote these entries; your job is to FALSIFY them, not confirm. Read-only on entries and sources. Write only your report file.

Standards: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (read it first). Every rule there is a check.

For EVERY entry in scope:
1. Every number, definition, table value and quote appears at the cited PDF page (and printed page) and means the same thing. Open the pages yourself; do not trust the entry.
2. Attribution: plain text is the book author's own statement. Anything else must be labelled "Eric's baseline:", "Eric's review:" or "Inference:". Flag any unlabelled claim the author did not make, any "why it works" mechanism the author did not give, and any invented example.
3. Confidence: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics, so challenge every `proven`. Soviet-era or single-lab findings and prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for anecdotes. `contested` needs a stated reason.
4. "When NOT to apply" is present and substantive.
5. Duplicates: flag any entry that restates an existing vault entry (grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library`) without a new angle.
6. Missing: up to 5 important ideas in the covered pages that no entry captures.

Output (Markdown): a table with one row per entry: file | verdict (GO / FIX / NO-GO) | problem, quoting the entry and the source with its page | exact correction. For GO rows, list what you checked ("checked: 2.5x at PDF 23 / p.12"). Then the missing list. Then an overall verdict: PROMOTE, GO AFTER FIXES (list them), or NO-GO.

The corrections above add the ones that matter.

## Challenge to the atomizer's confidence report (0 contested, 36 of 37 supported)

- **No entry needs `contested`** between library sources. The Menaspa 2017 rolling-averages paper in the vault is about ACWR and injury, a different question, and does not conflict.
- **`supported` holds as the practitioner-course ceiling for the frameworks,** with one change: `heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience.md` should be `untested` (the entry itself calls it untested opinion, and the rewrite leaves no evidence beyond Weber's view).

Corrections above.
- **Commercial interest is under-flagged.** SpeedSig is Weber's product (Podcast 1 00:00:47 to 00:00:53). It supplies the decisive evidence in the evidence-stacking hamstring case, the innovator example in the adoption-curve talk, and the branding of the K–B workbook; the Structured Thinking PDF p.1 describes itself as the basis of a protocol "used in the SpeedSig Primer Course". Only lead-with-the-recipient flags it.
- **Weber's own cited science is unflagged where entries lean on it:** decision fatigue and willpower depletion (Webinar 3 Part I), "research shows that after 15 to 20 minutes, people are off on other tangents" (Podcast 3 00:03:04 to 00:03:11), and neuro-linguistic programming (Webinar 3 Part II 00:05:40). None is sourced; the entries that use them should say so (set-communication, translate-metrics).

## Eric's baseline check

Every "Eric's baseline:" line was traced. All but two are supported by `docs/method-baseline.md`.
- **Not in the baseline (claims about Eric's practice):** (1) capability-audit: "Eric's own gap analysis names the department's reporting model as currently under-specified" (the baseline has this only as Tension #2, the baseline author's observation). (2) meeting-typology: the Inference that the baseline "shows [retrospective review] happening informally". Both are marked FIX above.
- **Inferred course-team positions written as Eric's own:** eras claim ("Eric's own course material states a skepticism"; baseline line 29 is Inferred, speaker unconfirmed), cm2 (Vermeil "compass", line 82, Inferred), monitoring-vs-testing and rolling-baselines (weekly tracking preference, line 47, Inferred), meeting-typology (annual plan, line 149, Inferred). Wording is close to the baseline's own, so these are not verdict-changing, but the promote step should append "(course team, Inferred)" to each.
- **Absence claim stated as baseline fact:** reliability-vs-sensitivity ("no MDC95, SWC, or typical-error figure for mRSI appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus"). Marked FIX.

Grep of `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` for kaigi, stoplight, decision gate, decision log, means/modality, evidence stack, measurement vs inference, DIKW, grey zone, rolling average/EWMA, protocol drift, tenth man, adoption curve, knowledge-behaviour, Weber/Old Bull: **no duplicates.** Reciprocal-link suggestions:
- `framework--decision-gate-five-elements` and `framework--stoplight-storytelling-format` ↔ `research-papers/robertson-2017-red-amber-or-green-athlete-monitoring-in-team-sport-the-need-for-decision-support-systems.md`

Each person writes independently before discussion; the answers become the contingency plan (Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure.pdf p.3). The most directly usable RTP tool in the course, and no entry has it.

Your decision is, do they need to play or not?" (Lab 2E transcript 00:03:00 to 00:03:30). **Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Harries' own stated reason is narrower: the middle-phase time is set "to equate to a given speed through that middle distance... that's going to correspond to the athlete's max velocity" (~18:18-18:29) - i.e. it gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity.

-**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

+**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps. In the strides, recovery lengthens to a walk-back between reps, with a check-in conversation before speed is raised (Part 3 19:47-20:12).

-**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.

entries.description:
Run multiple commands in ONE call. Every command's output is auto-indexed into the knowledge base; if you also pass `queries`, the matching sections come back in the same round trip so a follow-up search call is not needed.

Concurrency parallelizes the FETCH phase (run-the-commands). The DERIVATION phase — turning raw output into an answer — still belongs in code: add a processing command that consumes the indexed output and prints only the answer, so the raw bytes never enter your conversation (Think-in-Code, same principle as the sandbox tool).

WHEN:
  - You have 3+ related commands you would otherwise run sequentially (multi-issue lookups, git log + git diff + git blame, multi-file reads, multi-region cloud queries)
  - You want to gather AND query in one round trip — pass `queries` so the matching sections come back inline
  - You want to parallelize I/O-bound work — pass `concurrency` 2-8 (network calls, gh CLI, cloud APIs, multi-repo git reads)
  - The combined output is large enough that piping it through ctx_search later would itself be expensive — let auto-index + inline queries do both in one shot

WHEN NOT:
  - Single command with no follow-up query — run it in the sandbox tool directly
  - CPU-bound or stateful commands — keep concurrency at 1 (npm test, build, lint, port-binding servers, lock-file holders, anything that races on the same resource)

RETURNS:
  Auto-indexed section list per command label, plus top matches per query (when `queries` is passed). Raw output is NOT echoed in full — only the matched windows. Concurrency>1 switches each command to its own per-command timeout (no shared budget); concurrency=1 preserves the legacy shared-budget cascading-skip-on-timeout path. Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches; keep at 1 for CPU work or shared-state commands; lower the value when target hosts enforce per-IP rate limits.

EXAMPLE: ctx_batch_execute(
  commands: [
    {label: "issue 1", command: "gh issue view 1"},
    {label: "issue 2", command: "gh issue view 2"},
    {label: "summarize", command:… [truncated]

commands.description: Commands to execute as a batch. Output is labeled with the section header. Default order is sequential; pass concurrency>1 to run in parallel (output stays in input order).

queries.description: Search queries to extract information from indexed output. Use 5-8 comprehensive queries. Each returns top 5 matching sections with full content. This is your ONLY chance — put ALL your questions here. No follow-up calls needed.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs. With concurrency=1, the value (when set) is a shared budget across commands; with concurrency>1, it is applied per-command.

concurrency.description: Max commands to run in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches (network, gh, curl, multi-repo git reads). Keep at 1 for CPU-bound (npm test, build, lint) or stateful commands (ports, locks). >1 switches to per-command timeouts (no shared budget) and individual `(timed out)` blocks instead of cascading skip.

Read a file into a sandboxed FILE_CONTENT variable and run code over it. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation — the file bytes stay in the sandbox.

Think-in-Code applied to file-level analysis: Reading the whole file means every byte enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-… [truncated]

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

project.description: Project scope. Default (omit): this session's project — auto-resolved from the host adapter. 'global': span every project in the shared store (cross-project recall). <absolute-path>: scope to that specific project directory.

00:01:04** fundamentally a basic overview of how you run your leadership group and how you operate within your

**00:01:04–00:01:09** staff. So developing a common language. Every domain has its own vocabulary, priorities, communication

**00:01:09–00:01:16** norms, etc. If we don't have a common language, then communication becomes translation. And that

**00:01:16–00:01:21** means that we have to actively think about what we're saying and how we're saying it. Think about

**00:01:21–00:01:27** working in another language. I think in English, I have to translate it to Spanish, I have to speak

**00:01:27–00:01:33** about it in Spanish, hear the answer back in Spanish, decode it back to English to think about

**00:01:33–00:01:38** it. That's a lot of work. And if you're doing the same thing, trying to communicate complex

**00:01:40–00:01:44** concepts and the like to coaches, staff, whatever, it's really important that you

# The Capability and Workflow Audit Matrix

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from what a department has to what it produces and who acts on it. The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain: rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring; or by question: hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

# Decision Gates: Five Elements That Turn Data Into a Decision

**What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated**: named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria**: pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options**: progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership**: who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step**: the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("First clinical review happens within X hours," "Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).

**When to apply** — Any recurring return-to-play, load-progression, or technology-adoption decision that currently gets re-litigated case by case. **Eric's baseline:** "KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing" is named as a departmental operating principle, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this framework is a direct template for building that missing protocol, element by element.

**When NOT to apply** — A decision gate is indefensible without knowing how noisy the underlying measurement is; Weber's own next lab makes this explicit: see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the statistics a gate's criteria depend on. **Example** — Weber's own lab task: build one performance gate (e.g., speed-exposure progression) and one rehab gate (e.g., hamstring return-to-run), each specifying key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]: the statistical foundation a gate's criteria need. # The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit

**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: pathways break "not because the people are bad at jobs, but the process has a gap. Steps are not defined and people's roles within those steps are not defined" (6D transcript 00:00:42 to 00:00:52), and naming the stages lets a team "name exactly where your pathway is breaking" (00:00:57 to 00:01:06). Inference: this is the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]], applied to a single decision's pipeline.

**When to apply** — Weber's own stated practical use: trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it (10:52–12:11). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, with no sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently documented [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment; Load monitoring and GPS]. **Inference:** Weber's expertise-gap point, that someone needs to set and review the thresholds a measurement is judged against, including software defaults, lands directly on that named gap; this framework gives it a specific owner-and-process fix rather than leaving it as a general observation.

**When NOT to apply** — This framework audits the pipeline's structure; it does not itself validate whether a given threshold or software default is the right one, only that someone should be reviewing it. It also assumes a decision pathway already exists to be traced: for a genuinely new signal with no established pathway, the encoding and integration frameworks (see [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]]) are the prior step.

**Example** — Weber's communication-gap framing: leading with a clear recommendation first, and putting supporting technical detail in a form the recipient can actually use, rather than requiring the recipient to extract the recommendation from technical language themselves (05:32–08:54), the same discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] applied specifically at the decision-pathway's communication stage.

**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]]: the department-level companion to this pipeline-level audit. [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]]: the communication-gap discipline this framework names as stage four. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]: the formal structure for stage five's authority and action.

# Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal

**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision, per the lesson summary: does staff have enough independent, relevant information to act (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is treated as one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). **Inference:** the likely reason combining sources helps is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives, illustrated with Weber's soccer-knee and hamstring anecdotes (02:20–17:35), is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive.

# The Integration Problem: Five Break Points Between Data and Decision

**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap**: teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap**: no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gradient**: a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit**: the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence; per the lesson summary, Weber frames this as a shared responsibility, with practitioners sharing responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information; **(5) process absence**: missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's core claim, stated directly, is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). **Inference:** naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that good work isn't landing into a specific, auditable question, which of the five links actually failed.

**When to apply** — Reviewing a past decision where technically sound information did not change the outcome, or auditing a department's current pathway for a specific recurring signal (e.g., a fatigue flag, an asymmetry finding). Weber's own audit question directly names the exercise: "you need to ask whether your data has ever directly changed a major decision, and whether you can trace the path from collection to action" (cheat sheet p.1). **Eric's baseline:** KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** Weber's audit question is a useful test to run against that specific gap.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own account of a past bone-stress-injury case, where he says he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use, is a personal anecdote illustrating the communication point; it does not establish a general injury-prediction rule from training surface, and the transcript cannot verify the causal claim (Video Lab 6A summary, 13:14–15:38). **Example** — Weber's authority-gradient distinction: overriding a technical recommendation, in the course's words, "sometimes that is necessary, but it should happen transparently and with explanation" (cheat sheet p.1); the failure mode is the silent override, not the override itself.

**Related** — [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]]: the next-stage problem (same information, different disciplinary lens) that this framework's language gap connects to. [[framework--decision-pathway-six-stages-five-gaps]]: a parallel, more granular breakdown of the data-to-decision pipeline. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]]: where the authority gradient is resolved for medical/performance overlap specifically.

# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix

**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). **Why it works** — Weber gives the grid two uses: development (spot skill gaps, plan CPD: Lab 1B Part 2 summary 02:10 to 04:04) and selection (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:07:40 to 00:08:02: misaligned staff "need to be managed out"; Lab_1b blog p.4: "Make tough calls on the misaligned"). **Inference:** splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions, a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person likely needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push, consistent with Weber's own worked contrast (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

# Measurement vs. Inference

**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples, per the lesson summary: calling a lower countermovement-jump result neurological fatigue, or a GPS change tissue stress: neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated reasons: overstating certainty "is what drives coaches crazy" (Lab_2a PDF p.2; transcript 00:02:09 to 00:02:17), and because "humans are an incredibly redundant system" the same output can hide different strategies (Lab_2a PDF p.2), so an inference has to be built by triangulation to a probability, not asserted (PDF p.3; transcript 00:03:20 to 00:04:01). **Inference:** collapsing the distinction likely lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example, what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise: see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02), the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]: combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]: whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]]: the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build

**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review: the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb (decide, diagnose, inform, or build) plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).

**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running **decide** structure on a **diagnose** problem, or vice versa). **Eric's baseline:** the course team's material treats the annual plan as a roadmap adapted as circumstances change [method-baseline.md line 149, Inferred]. **Inference:** the baseline records no after-action or retrospective format, so the AAR mode (cheat sheet p.2: 15 to 30 min, blameless, learning points plus procedure changes plus owners) would be new practice at Baylor, not a formalization of an existing one.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no evidence that naming a mode improves meeting outcomes beyond his own stated experience; this is a proposed practice, not a tested intervention. It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs; that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda. # Stoplight Storytelling

**What it is** — A short, repeatable presentation format for bringing a decision to a group: state the question or headline first (rather than opening with data that has no stated purpose); show status using green (go), amber (hold/monitor), or red (stop/change); present at most one chart, readable immediately, that addresses whether an observed difference is meaningful relative to measurement error, normal variation, and other convergent evidence; and close with a requested direction (start/stop/change) plus one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 00:00–04:25; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Presentation rules: keep the message short, label axes and differences clearly, avoid dual axes and complex charts that require extended explanation, never bring multiple charts, multiple requests, or brand-new information into the moment, and give every status, including amber, a next action or review date (04:25–06:23). A roughly two-minute presentation is Weber's own benchmark, though he notes novel or complex issues may need pre-reading or a separate meeting instead (06:23–06:43). Timing is given two ways: about two minutes per slide (3C transcript 00:06:23 to 00:06:28; template p.2; cheat sheet p.2 "2 min per slide") and about five minutes per person, five presentations in 30 minutes (00:07:30 to 00:07:38).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to keep a sequence of presentations in one meeting from expanding into long, unfocused discussions, and to let staff present more autonomously once the shared format is understood (06:56–07:54). **Inference:** forcing one chart and one request likely removes the two most common ways a presentation drifts, adding more evidence than the room can process in the time available, and leaving the ask implicit so no decision actually gets made.

**When to apply** — Any recurring review where multiple practitioners each need to bring a status update that may require a decision: a weekly return-to-play review, a load-monitoring standup, or a technology-adoption check-in. Pairs directly with the kaigi format's evidence-precision rule (see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]) as the visual layer of the same discipline.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's two-minute benchmark and single-chart rule are explicitly not meant for novel or complex issues, which he says may need pre-reading or a dedicated meeting instead (06:23–06:43); **Inference:** forcing a genuinely complex, multi-variable problem into stoplight format would risk the same false simplicity the framework is otherwise designed to avoid (see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]). The timing and efficiency claims are Weber's own practice examples, not validated thresholds.

**Example** — The course's slide template (Lab_3c_Stoplight_Storytelling_Slide_Template.pdf p.1 to p.2): headline decision question; one stoplight status with a one-line reason; one chart with baseline, current, change, SEM and MDC95; at most two pieces of convergent evidence; one ask written as a verb (Start/Stop/Change/Limit/Continue); owner, action, due, review; footer "2 minutes total. If it needs explaining, it's the wrong meeting type."

**Related** — [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]: the closing record this format requires. [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]: the meeting format this presentation style is built to feed. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]: the caution against over-simplifying a genuinely complex decision.

# Strategy Is the Highway, Tactics Are Changing Lanes

**What it is** — Weber's delegation model: **strategy** is the department's direction, standards, and the key questions it cares about, described as "the highway"; **tactics** are the day-to-day choices staff make within that direction (which tool to deploy, how to adjust tests, timing, and exposure, how to respond to what they see), described as "changing lanes" (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1–2). The stated goal is to give staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (p.2). He restates the same model in Webinar 3 Part III as a direct delegation rule: the leader names the destination and boundaries, staff choose tactics within them, with more discretion given to an experienced colleague than a new hire, and explicit criteria for which decisions must be escalated (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 03:56–06:30).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated goal is that the model gives staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.2). Weber's stated mechanism: clear intent lets staff know "what can I make a decision on and what do I need to push up the chain", and staff without direction "become disillusioned. Their behavior will change", while micromanagement costs the leader control of time (Webinar 3 Part III transcript 00:05:18 to 00:06:30).

**When to apply** — Structuring how much autonomy a staff member has over test selection, session adjustments, or reporting choices, especially as a department scales past a size where informal alignment happens naturally. **Eric's baseline:** the Playbook's stated peer-department framing for Applied Performance ("enabling" other departments to answer their own questions) is not fully reconciled with a support-staff framing that also appears in the same corpus ("helping program and plan the training") [method-baseline.md Tensions #2]. **Inference:** naming the specific highway (standards, questions Applied Performance owns) versus the lanes (tactical choices left to individual practitioners) is a direct way to resolve that ambiguity in practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no method for determining where the highway's boundaries should sit for a given department or decision type; that judgment call is left entirely to the leader. It is also not a substitute for the formal escalation criteria a decision gate provides (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) when the stakes are high enough to need a documented pass/fail/borderline threshold rather than a general delegation boundary.

**Example** — A first-year graduate gets "one or two lanes max"; a 10-year colleague gets "the full six lane highway" (Webinar 3 Part III transcript 00:04:38 to 00:04:51; Lab_3D blog p.1: "six-lane highway ... but nobody drives off-road").

**Related** — [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]: the audit this delegation model is embedded in. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]: the more formal structure for higher-stakes decisions. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]]: the companion communication rules from the same Webinar 3 material.

# The Tech Stack Reality Check

**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability**: can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that many performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department will, in his words, "chase noise and call it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.

# Stoplight Storytelling

**What it is** — A short, repeatable presentation format for bringing a decision to a group: state the question or headline first (rather than opening with data that has no stated purpose); show status using green (go), amber (hold/monitor), or red (stop/change); present at most one chart, readable immediately, that addresses whether an observed difference is meaningful relative to measurement error, normal variation, and other convergent evidence; and close with a requested direction (start/stop/change) plus one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 00:00–04:25; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Presentation rules: keep the message short, label axes and differences clearly, avoid dual axes and complex charts that require extended explanation, never bring multiple charts, multiple requests, or brand-new information into the moment, and give every status, including amber, a next action or review date (04:25–06:23). A roughly two-minute presentation is Weber's own benchmark, though he notes novel or complex issues may need pre-reading or a separate meeting instead (06:23–06:43). Timing is given two ways: about two minutes per slide (3C transcript 00:06:23 to 00:06:28; template p.2; cheat sheet p.2 "2 min per slide") and about five minutes per person, five presentations in 30 minutes (00:07:30 to 00:07:38).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to keep a sequence of presentations in one meeting from expanding into long, unfocused discussions, and to let staff present more autonomously once the shared format is understood (06:56–07:54). **Inference:** forcing one chart and one request likely removes the two most common ways a presentation drifts, adding more evidence than the room can process in the time available, and leaving the ask implicit so no decision actually gets made.

**When to apply** — Any recurring review where multiple practitioners each need to bring a status update that may require a decision: a weekly return-to-play review, a load-monitoring standup, or a technology-adoption check-in. Pairs directly with the kaigi format's evidence-precision rule (see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]) as the visual layer of the same discipline.

The timing and efficiency claims are Weber's own practice examples, not validated thresholds.

**Example** — The course's slide template (Lab_3c_Stoplight_Storytelling_Slide_Template.pdf p.1 to p.2): headline decision question; one stoplight status with a one-line reason; one chart with baseline, current, change, SEM and MDC95; at most two pieces of convergent evidence; one ask written as a verb (Start/Stop/Change/Limit/Continue); owner, action, due, review; footer "2 minutes total. # Choose a Mentor Above You Who Has Worked in Elite Sport

**What it is** — Weber's rule: a mentor should sit above you on the knowledge axis (practitioner or operator) and have worked at the level you aim for (Olympic, NFL, EPL, AFL); your main mentor cannot be someone who has never worked in sport (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:06:10 to 00:07:07; Lab_1b PDF p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated reason: elite sport's "the accountability process, the detail, the timing, the tempo" cannot be learned from someone who has not worked in it (00:07:07 to 00:07:13).

**When to apply** — Assigning a mentor to a new hire, intern, or staff member being developed toward more responsibility, when there is a real choice between a mentor who has worked in elite sport and one who has not. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's proposed intern curriculum is explicitly adapting a Clemson Olympic-sports model "to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]. Inference: for Baylor interns, the mentor pool should include staff who have worked at the level the intern is aiming for.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Weber's stated opinion, not a tested claim; he gives no comparison of outcomes between mentors who have worked in elite sport and those who have not, and no guidance for cases where no such mentor is available above you. In that case the choice is between an imperfect option and no mentor at all, which this heuristic does not address.

**Example** — Weber's framing places this immediately after his call for aspiring leaders to start practicing leadership before they hold the title (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 02:36–03:59), positioning mentor selection as part of a deliberate leadership-development pipeline rather than an incidental pairing.

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]]: the companion practice for identifying who needs a mentor. [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]: the grid this selection criterion sits inside.

# Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology

**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own is, in Weber's words, "the most powerful piece of performance tech you own", yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example, per the transcript (which renders "strength and conditioning" as "straight conditioning," an evident ASR error): "I've been a [strength and] conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). **Inference:** a department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.

**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own gap analysis names sport-specific data dictionaries and Baylor-specific technology workflows as unfinished, prioritized work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3]. **Inference:** that work depends on exactly this computer/coding capability existing on staff, not just on the vendor tools themselves.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is careful to say "you don't need to become a programmer" (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1); this is not a claim that every S&C coach must learn to code. Inference: the department's analytic ceiling is set by whoever's computer skill is highest. It also doesn't specify which skills matter most (spreadsheets vs. dashboards vs. scripting) or how to build them; it names the gap, not the curriculum.

**Example** — Weber's own audit question set for this category: what computer do you actually have, what do you use beyond spreadsheets, and can you run data workflows or dashboards when needed (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]: the audit this claim is drawn from. [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]: why computer skill is the bottleneck between data and decisions.

# Ask Staff About Their CPD to Surface Both Support Needs and Ambition

**What it is** — Weber's suggested practice: ask staff directly about their continuing professional development (CPD) and invite brief presentations about something they recently learned (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21). He pairs this with a related opening exercise, from a colleague's 60-second exercise for a leadership group: write down the five things that could stop this from working (00:01:26 to 00:01:45), as a way to get people examining their own contribution and the team's bottlenecks.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated reason: asking staff to present "starts to show you where they're at", and he uses it as a check on staff who may be handbrakes (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:04:04 to 00:04:58). **Inference:** the same conversation can also separate a knowledge gap from a motivation gap, which maps onto the knowledge x behaviour matrix's two axes (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's proposed intern curriculum already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4]. **Inference:** a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no structure for how often to ask, what to do with the answer, or how to handle a staff member who cannot name any recent CPD; this is a prompt, not a full performance-management process. It also should not be the sole input into a personnel decision (see the caution in [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**Example** — Weber's own framing, per the lesson summary: asking staff about CPD and inviting a short presentation on something recently learned, as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]: the grid this practice is meant to inform. [[heuristic--choose-a-mentor-above-you-who-has-worked-in-elite-sport]]: the companion practice for staff who need external development support.

# Schedule Time to Ask What Could Break the System, Before It Does

**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). His stated reasoning: a team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (03:22–04:06), the same blind spot his structured-dissent practices (see [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]) are meant to catch inside a specific meeting, applied here as a standing habit rather than a one-off intervention.

**Why it works** — **Inference:** a system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system as staff, technology, and knowledge change treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup. Weber's stated reason: people, technology and information change, so a working system drifts, and "what seems nice and stable ... may unravel at the point when you don't need it to" (Podcast 6 transcript 00:12:12 to 00:13:36).

**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. **Eric's baseline:** a three-phase roadmap ends with an annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]. **Inference:** this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the question of what could break the system, not only an update-the-document pass.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review, only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.

**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]: the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]: the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's proposed intern curriculum already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4]. **Inference:** a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.

**Example** — Weber's own framing, per the lesson summary: asking staff about CPD and inviting a short presentation on something recently learned, as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).

**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). **Why it works** — **Inference:** a system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. **Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: performance-technology-and-leadership
book: old-bull-performance-course--old-bull
chapter: "2C"
topic: rolling averages mask slow real change
category: [monitoring, reliability]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Rolling Averages Answer "Drifting This Week?", Not "Improved This Phase?"

**What it is** — Weber's specific caution inside the monitoring-vs-testing framework (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]): rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are excellent at answering "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week," but they are not designed to answer "did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1–2). His fix: long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs. post, block vs. block), not continuous smoothing (p.2).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** a rolling window is, by construction, always chasing the most recent values. If an athlete's true capacity drifts down gradually over a training block, a rolling average would likely track that drift and never flag it as a deviation, because the reference point itself has quietly moved with the athlete. The same window that makes short-term monitoring useful (fast reaction to recent change) is what makes it blind to slow change. Weber himself states the effect (rolling averages answer a different question than phase-level testing) without spelling out this mechanism.

**When to apply** — Any metric tracked with a rolling window or EWMA for daily/weekly monitoring that is also, informally or formally, being used to answer a phase-level question of whether the athlete's capacity actually improved. **Eric's baseline:** weekly tracking is stated as preferred over infrequent, once-a-phase testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the specific mechanism behind the broader tension flagged in [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] between Weber's framework and that stated preference.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument against rolling averages for their intended purpose (short-term status and load-adjustment decisions); it is a warning against also treating the same rolling number as evidence of long-term program effectiveness. It also does not specify how wide a rolling window should be for a given metric, only that no window substitutes for a genuine pre/post or block/block comparison.

**Example** — Weber's own instruction: to evaluate a training phase, compare defined phases or time points (pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two) rather than relying on the continuous smoothing used for weekly monitoring (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]: the parent framework this heuristic sits inside. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]: the statistics for deciding whether any observed change, rolling or block-based, is real.

# Agree Which Channel Carries What, and When, Before the Pressure Arrives

**What it is** — Weber's set of communication rules meant to be settled in advance rather than negotiated in the moment: specify which channel carries each kind of information and what behavior is expected on it; for injuries specifically, state in advance when the coach receives a provisional update and when a more specific medical update may follow; agree the timing and form of post-training reports, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats; mark messages by urgency or purpose; and make meeting invitations state their objective, length, and required preparation, with project assignments stating the deliverable, deadline, expected quality, and people to consult, plus expected response times (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 06:11–10:09). In Part III he adds three more standing practices from the same "discipline equals freedom" chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): document routine work so it is clear who handles equipment, session prep, data collection, and testing; remove avoidable ambiguity by stating a meeting's purpose, deadline, and each person's role; and schedule regular feedback check-ins, addressing performance issues promptly and asking staff for feedback on the leader's own leadership (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–09:15).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism ties directly to attention management: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05). His example: a head coach, doctor, and strength coach may all ask about training load from entirely different concerns and technical backgrounds, so the leader needs pre-agreed shared language and channel norms to respond efficiently rather than re-deriving the right answer for each asker every time (00:59–02:46).

**When to apply** — Setting up communication norms for a new season, a new coach relationship, or a newly formed interdisciplinary group, particularly around injury updates, where ambiguity about timing is most costly. **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the channel-and-timing layer that makes that advisory information actually arrive when it is needed.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's claims about cognitive effects and communication methods are presented as his own management practice, not independently validated outcomes (Webinar 3 Part II summary caveat). This is also not a substitute for the decision-gate timeframes in [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]], which cover the higher-stakes case of formal go/hold/stop decisions rather than routine reporting cadence. Inference: Weber's mechanism rests on a decision-fatigue or willpower-depletion account he does not source (Webinar 3 Part I transcript 00:02:52 to 00:03:17, 00:09:03 to 00:09:11); that literature is contested, so treat the time-saving rationale as his experience, not an established effect.

**Example** — Weber's military-analogy caution in Part I: he explicitly warns that military and sport stakes differ, using the analogy only to illustrate that rehearsed communication routines let a team act without inventing a process under pressure: in one AFL case, coach and performance staff adjusted a training session mid-session (dropping a drill, extending another, pulling named players on exposure) because they shared enough technical language to estimate consequences for specific players in real time (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 05:05–09:03). Untested anecdote, Weber's own account.

**Related** — [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]: the underlying chain this set of rules extends. [[heuristic--translate-metrics-into-coaches-vocabulary]]: the vocabulary-specific version of this same discipline. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]: the delegation-boundary companion from the same Webinar.

# Assign Someone to Argue the Other Side Before You Decide

**What it is** — Weber describes an International Rugby Union coach (and CEOs he has observed) who stated a problem, then sat silent until staff had spoken, so the leader's view did not bias the decision (3D transcript 00:06:25 to 00:07:08; Podcast 6 00:05:04 to 00:06:03; Lab_3D blog p.2: "pose the problem…then sit quietly"). His own practice is to assign one staff member to "argue the opposite. Find data, find anything to argue the opposite" (3D 00:07:24 to 00:07:37), the same idea behind the "tenth man" device from *World War Z* he also names (assign someone to formally argue against the group's favored explanation). He cites de Bono's six hats but says he has never used it in a meeting; his own version is to rule that "for the next five minutes, you can only speak data" (Podcast 6 00:06:34 to 00:07:25). He also describes a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail (04:59–06:34).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated reasoning, per the lesson summary, is that a team sharing one process can still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 03:22–04:06). **Inference:** a leader who speaks first likely sets an anchor that makes dissent socially costly for everyone after them; formally assigning the dissenting role removes that social cost, since the person arguing against the plan is doing their job, not breaking rank.

**When to apply** — High-stakes or hard-to-reverse decisions, especially ones the group has converged on quickly or that fit a familiar pattern the department has not recently questioned. Weber's own recurring calf-injury anecdote (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is his illustration of what happens when dissent has no formal channel and instead depends on finding the right messenger after the fact (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for which decisions warrant an assigned dissenter versus ordinary discussion. **Inference:** using it for every routine call would likely slow decision-making without adding much value. The film and historical references (World War Z, six hats) are illustrations of the practice, not evidence for its effectiveness in a performance department, and the calf-injury anecdote is a personal account that does not establish the training change's actual effect on injury rates.

**Example** — Weber's own account, per the lesson summary: a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail, rather than stating a view first and then asking for objections to it (04:59–06:34).

**Related** — [[heuristic--assign-meeting-ownership-to-develop-staff]]: the companion staff-development practice from the same lab. [[heuristic--review-the-system-on-a-schedule]]: the broader practice of scheduling this kind of challenge proactively rather than only after a problem appears.

# Report in the Coach's Existing Words, Without Losing the Link to the Measurement

**What it is** — Weber's recommendation: replace technical language with terms the audience already uses, while keeping the connection back to the underlying measurement intact. His AFL example: he and a coach agreed on verbal running categories, then used those categories in reporting rather than leading with speed units (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 01:09–06:11). He recommends explaining processes in plain terms, documenting them where useful, offering coaches short reference sheets, and learning a given coach's preferred words and report format early in the season, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats of information (07:48–08:39).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: without a common language "communication becomes translation", with a high "mental cost" (Webinar 3 Part II transcript 00:01:09 to 00:01:50), and a coach who hears their own words back gains confidence in the report (00:05:55 to 00:06:00). He sources the second point to neuro-linguistic programming (00:05:40), which has little empirical support; treat it as his experience. **Inference:** agreeing verbal categories once removes the translation step from every later report, the same recipient-question discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] and the failure mode named in [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]].

**When to apply** — Building or revising any coach-facing report template, and specifically at the start of a season or with a new coach, before habits and expectations have set. **Eric's baseline:** standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]. **Inference:** this heuristic argues the template design process should start with the coach's own vocabulary, established early, rather than a generic vendor-report format.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not argue for dropping technical precision internally among performance and medical staff, only for translating it at the coach-facing layer; the underlying measurement and its documented reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) should not be diluted, only re-expressed. It also assumes a coach's preferred vocabulary is knowable and stable enough to build a template around. **Inference:** for a new coach, that may take a full season to establish.

**Example** — Weber's specific practice: verbal running categories, agreed once with the coach ("jog, stride, sprint, gut run", 00:02:37 to 00:03:22), used consistently in reporting instead of raw speed-band units (01:09–06:11).

**Related** — [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]]: the general communication principle this applies to coaches specifically. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]]: the companion rules for when and how coach-facing information is delivered.
